headline: US midterm voting begins with markets already unsettled: the Nasdaq-100 is in a correction, oil is above $100 on the Iran conflict, and central banks keep raising rates. Healthcare is dominated by a biotech bankruptcy, a wave of biosimilar and manufacturing deals, and rising premiums.

paragraphs.text: The clearest distress story is Karyopharm. Fierce Biotech and Endpoints report that the multiple myeloma drugmaker has filed for Chapter 11 and lined up Ayrmid, the company that previously tried to buy bluebird, as lead bidder in a court-supervised auction that could become a hematology merger. BioPharma Dive notes the company recently struck a forbearance deal to push off debt payments, so this looks like a debt-driven sale rather than a strategic one. For credit investors in small commercial-stage biotech, it is a reminder that a marketed drug does not protect a leveraged balance sheet.

paragraphs.text: Contract manufacturing and biosimilars are the main deal themes. Endpoints says Merck KGaA is exiting its CDMO business and selling five US sites and about 1,100 employees to Lonza, with financial terms undisclosed. Fresenius and WuXi Biologics agreed a broad biosimilars pact that, per Fierce Pharma, could take Fresenius to as many as 66 molecules aimed at originator products worth more than €370 billion. BioPharma Dive adds that Keytruda biosimilars are coming as Merck's patent cliff nears, but may struggle to win wide uptake. Separately, Fierce Pharma reports FDA inspection write-ups at Hansoh in China (sterilization issues) and Samsung Biologics in Korea (data falsification), which matter for anyone underwriting outsourced manufacturing. AbbVie also disclosed a deal with Beijing-based Brise for two preclinical migraine programs, a deal Brise said dates from 2024, and Barron's argues the way to play China's biotech rise is through US drug stocks.

paragraphs.text: Regulatory and clinical news was mixed. The FDA granted uniQure's Huntington's gene therapy priority review, with a decision date of May 1 and an advisory committee planned. It also approved Inovio's Voceryq for a rare HPV-driven airway disease, after an earlier scare over the accelerated path, and Endpoints says Inovio's stock surged. The agency approved a generic HIV prevention shot to widen access in lower-income countries. On the negative side, the FDA put a partial hold on Bright Minds' seizure drug over preclinical toxicity in mice, and the stock fell sharply. Novartis walked away from an $800 million BioArctic neuroscience collaboration after 14 months, and Teva stopped a trial for futility. InventisBio reported a phase 3 psoriasis win for its TYK2 inhibitor, and Tiziana's MS drug hit its endpoints, though the higher dose missed a neuroinflammation goal. Vertex's third-quarter coverage points to Crinetics integration shaping its outlook, but the list gives little detail.

paragraphs.text: Earnings were uneven. BioPharma Dive says AstraZeneca is launching a restructuring program, Alnylam sold off on worries about a top drug, and Regeneron was rewarded for a record quarter. Bayer shares jumped after a pharma recovery led it to raise guidance, and Philips rose on stronger profitability, per the Journal. Community Health Systems lowered its 2026 earnings forecast, Healthcare Dive says, as uninsured patients who had been on ACA plans sought care and some elective surgeries were deferred. That fits the broader affordability picture: the New York Times reports ACA premiums rising an average 13% for 2027 on top of an earlier steep increase, and KFF finds Medicare Part D premiums spiking about 50% on average. The Times also reports insurers withholding payment on emergency bills despite the surprise-billing law. The FTC has sent warning letters to 25 insurance marketers as enrollment opens, and UnitedHealthcare will drop prior authorization on more than 2,000 pediatric codes from Dec. 1. Fierce Healthcare says hospitals should not expect quick policy relief after the midterms, and Brigham and Women's nurses set an open-ended strike for Nov. 12.

paragraphs.text: Smaller items: Fierce Biotech says OpenAI-backed Biossil bought Theriva's deprioritized antibiotic-degrading enzyme portfolio for up to $91 million. Two venture funds closed early, Singapore's NSV at $53 million and NeoSci at $54.7 million, both for biotech. Athenahealth is opening patient records to Anthropic's Claude, and Zocdoc is opening its infrastructure to AI agents. Healthcare Dive reports the AMA wants liability for clinical AI shared across physicians, vendors and health systems. STAT reports a Washington state resident died of bird flu after exposure to infected cattle, the first such US death in a year, and the Times reports the administration plans to roll back pregnancy-related job protections.

paragraphs.text: The backdrop is a shaky AI trade going into Election Day. CNBC says the S&P 500 and Nasdaq opened November with losses as tech was sold on Monday, and MarketWatch says the Nasdaq-100 has fallen into its third correction this year, asking whether a bear market is next. CNBC also notes the S&P 500 posted a second straight losing month, but only because of a handful of stocks, and the average stock is having its best relative performance in decades. The Journal reports European chip shares falling after an Asian selloff in AI-exposed names, and the FT reports Nvidia telling cloud clients that most of their customers must be non-Chinese. The FT also warns that equity volatility risk is rising after a period of remarkable resilience. MarketWatch says a leveraged Nasdaq-100 ETF burned dip-buyers last month, and the Journal says AI investors are seeking downside protection.

paragraphs.text: Earnings added to the mood. MarketWatch says Apple fell 4.5% premarket on disappointment over its gross margin outlook and slowing services growth, with a worsening memory crunch cited even though iPhone demand is strong. The Journal calls Apple an AI safe haven that isn't cheap. Palantir's profit soared and, per the Journal, US commercial revenue passed government revenue, but MarketWatch says the stock fell because US commercial contract growth decelerated. DuPont swung to a $123 million third-quarter profit and lifted its outlook. Lufthansa turned cautious as fuel costs weigh despite strong demand.

paragraphs.text: Energy and geopolitics are driving rates. The FT reports oil steady around $106 after sharp declines, with traders watching the Middle East after the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on election eve, which Washington called defensive. The Journal says oil rebounded, lifting the dollar and Treasury and European yields, and pushing gold lower on rate-hike worries. European gas rebounded after an 8% drop. MarketWatch quotes oil strategist Jeff Currie saying it is time to take profits after this year's run while the structural supercycle remains intact. Saudi Aramco's third-quarter profit rose 9% despite attacks on pipelines and refineries, though the Times says Gulf economies have seen growth plunge in a year of war.

paragraphs.text: Central banks keep tightening. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, after materially revising up its inflation forecasts, and the Journal had flagged a deepening housing slump. The Journal says the Bank of England is expected to hike Thursday, joining the Fed, ECB and BoJ, each of which has raised at least once since the US-Iran war began. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October from 1.0%. The FT says Brussels wants eurozone nominees to succeed Christine Lagarde by Friday. US factory activity expanded, with the ISM index at 55.5 versus 54.5 in September. JPMorgan Asset Management's Bob Michele urged the Treasury to drop the 20-year ahead of the refunding.

The PBOC raised the FX reserve requirement ratio by 2 points to 6%, and the FT says regulators halted listings after the CSI 300 had its worst month in more than a decade. On the election, the FT reports voting has begun and an FT poll shows a big majority disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation. CNBC notes midterms have historically preceded a strong S&P 500 year, and the Journal flags health insurance as a sleeper inflation issue.

CNBC reports Blackstone president Jon Gray saying the buildout needs more equity as debt investors face concentration risk. FT Alphaville says AI is making credit default swaps relevant again, and separately questions what data-center construction delays mean for investors. MarketWatch notes a signal from the corporate bond market that has historically preceded big S&P 500 drawdowns, though the snippet doesn't say which signal. paragraphs.text: Primary-market evidence of caution: Bloomberg reports banks pulled a €550 million refinancing loan for Iqony, a European energy infrastructure and services company, for lack of investor interest amid wider market turmoil. It is described as another pulled deal in Europe's junk market, which suggests risk appetite is thinning for lower-rated borrowers.

paragraphs.text: Private credit looks steadier but more selective. InvestmentNews says demand holds firm while investors grow cautious. Fundraising continues: Neo raised ₹6,200 crore for its second private credit fund, Oklahoma Teachers made new private debt commitments, and Partners Group won a $510 million insurer mandate even as its US flagship reportedly left two-thirds of exit requests unmet, a sign of liquidity strain in evergreen vehicles. TLG Capital gave a credit facility to Nigeria's Koolboks, and the FT reports Security Benefit, Todd Boehly's insurer, has amassed billions in lending tied to his Beverly Hills project as regulators scrutinize insurers that lend to owner-affiliated companies.

The FDIC's inspector general says a mortgage expansion sank Tioga-Franklin through weak earnings, liquidity and capital problems, and the FDIC revised its directive on Old Glory Bank, now deemed adequately capitalized after a failed SPAC acquisition. paragraphs.text: The biggest deal is the all-stock combination of Marvell and Lumentum, described by the Times as a $115 billion merger and a bet on optical networking for AI data centers. MarketWatch says shares of both companies fell Monday and shareholders panned it, one calling it a trash offer, so the market reaction is an early test for stock-funded AI consolidation. Elsewhere, Cinven agreed to buy menopause specialist Theramex for €2.6 billion from Carlyle and PAI, which are selling at more than double their price four years ago, per the FT. Shell is selling an Australian gas stake to Abu Dhabi's XRG for $1.45 billion. Bloomberg says Emaar is studying a buyout of its $15 billion listed construction arm. Alternatives Watch reports a day of closings including Stonepeak's Castrol deal and Brookfield's $5.2 billion REIT take-private, and the FT says Brookfield is backing Drax's biomass-powered data center. Business Insider says DoorDash told staff not to connect with Instacart peers on LinkedIn, which hints at a deal but the list doesn't confirm one.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is a recurring subject. Proactive and Fortune both report analysts doubting a roughly $2 trillion valuation given its compute and data center costs, and Crain's says a Michigan data center's fate hinges on the listing. FT Alphaville points to Anthropic's risk factors. Anthropic also features as a partner: Hg agreed to back a new European AI transformation firm alongside it, per PEI. The sources are thin on figures. ElevenLabs' CEO says starting IPO prep in 2028 would be a good goal, and Neuracle Medical has begun A-share IPO tutoring in China's race for a first brain-computer interface listing. Saudi Arabia's CMA approved tighter IPO rules, the FT says Texas Stock Exchange is trying to challenge the New York exchanges, and China has paused listings. MoneyWeek says the best IPOs are often the hardest to buy.
